newsitem.title: UK: Adams challenge to Blair on N.Irish peace.
newsitem.headline: Adams challenge to Blair on N.Irish peace.

text.p: Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political wing, challenged new British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Friday to spearhead a drive to ensure Anglo-Irish peace for the next millenium.

Adams, whose guerrilla ally is waging an armed campaign against British rule in Northern Ireland, made the plea within hours of a Labour pledge that it will not water down conditions for Sinn Fein's entry into multi-party peace talks.
Mo Mowlam, the woman tipped to be the next Northern Ireland Secretary for Britain, said the Irish Republican Army must call a truce before Sinn Fein is given a talks seat.

Adams signalled no retreat from his demand for urgent entry into all-party talks when he spoke to reporters as counting went ahead at Belfast city hall for some of Northern Ireland seats in the British parliament, one of which he hoped to win.

He said Blair should seize "the opportunity to resolve the biggest single issue" besetting relations between the people of Britain and Ireland, "and to be the Prime Minister, not just to lead Britain into the next century, but to lead Ireland and Britain into a peaceful next century."

In Dublin, Irish prime minister John Bruton said a strong Labour government could, with Dublin, bring fresh drive to the search for Northern Ireland peace and it would be in a position to ease difficulties such as tension about controversial parades by pro-British Protestant.

It was a stunning victory, Bruton told reporters. "I think the fact that we now in Britain have a government with a strong majority will enable it to tackle issues with resolution in regard to Northern Ireland, to tackle the parades issue, to inject new urgency into the talks process.
"They will be doing it on the basis of a perspective that is shared with the Irish government," Bruton said.

Mowlam, one of the victors in a Labour landslide win that installed Tony Blair as British leader, said there would be no change in its refusal to talk with Sinn Fein while IRA fighters were on a war footing.

"We have made it very clear that none of my colleagues will have any contact with Sinn Fein while the IRA makes that impossible. However there is a door open there and they know the conditions through which they will facilitate others to pass through it," she said in a BBC radio interview.
Bruton agrees with Britain that an IRA truce must precede entry for Sinn Fein to multi-party talks that adjourned in deadlock in March.

In his final months in office, former Prime Minister John Major was criticised by Irish nationalists who accused him of shoring up his minority government with the help of pro-British Protestant leglisators from Northern Ireland.
